The Hanged Man determines what keeps your interest alive — a pause in which everything looks upside down and you can notice what you really want. The Wheel of Fortune answers with a sense of coming alive: life has taken a turn, and there is zest in it again.

**When the familiar collapses, it can be a door for you rather than an end.** Say that after many years in the same choir you are left without rehearsals, and for a while you simply listen to the silence in the evenings. Out of it, unexpectedly, something else grows: night walks with a voice recorder, recordings of birdsong, the sounds of the city. You don’t rush to fill the gap — and that is why you find what was never in your old schedule.

What you found in that pause is precious, and you want to stand up for it. Your way of relaxing is unusual now — night walks, celebrations spent alone, off-season trips — and the people around you don’t always understand it. You explain, you defend, you hold on to it out of principle. Meanwhile the wheel turns again: the interest cools, other wants wake up. Admitting this feels like defeat, as if the doubters had been right all along. And what once brought you back to life becomes a new familiar format, one you can only keep defending.

16-15-4.heading: Give a new passion solid walls
captions: Strong urge to go all in
paragraphs: When your old way of relaxing stops bringing you joy, you don’t patch it up — you tear it down. That is how the Tower works: the familiar format collapses all at once, with no long goodbyes. The Devil fuels the motivation — a strong pull towards a new pleasure you want to throw yourself into completely: with your time, your money, your body. The Emperor gives what remains afterwards: calm, once the new passion has clear boundaries — its own place, its own days, its own order.

**For you, a strong desire becomes a lasting joy once it takes shape.** Say that after falling out of love with loud parties you get swept up in horse riding. You find an instructor, choose your days, buy the gear — and for the first time in ages your leisure no longer depends on your mood. The pull hasn’t gone anywhere, but now it has a home, and in that home you feel at peace.

The form, though, can outlive the desire itself. A year’s membership is paid for, the saddle is bought, the schedule is set, and when your interest begins to cool, admitting it is almost impossible. So much has gone into it that leaving seems foolish, and you keep riding to schedule, irritated by any departure from it. The order holds firm, but there is less and less pleasure in it, like a kingdom where everything is under control and everything has dried up. The resolve with which you once tore down the old ends up locked inside what you built.

16-21-10.heading: From a cramped routine into the wide world
captions: Revived by a turn of fate
paragraphs: Your free time widens in leaps. The Tower breaks a cramped routine that has long outlived itself: the same café every Friday, one series everybody watches, the country house every weekend. The World shapes the desire — you want life to become wide again, and its different parts, trips, crafts, people, to come together into one picture. The Wheel of Fortune answers with a sense of coming alive: you feel that fate has turned and something is happening up ahead again.

**Breaking out of a cramped routine opens your way to a large, connected life.** Say your usual trip is cancelled and turns into a week in an unfamiliar city. There you happen upon a potters’ workshop, and back home a circle of people with the same passion appears. One thing leads to another, and out of a chance turn grows a new part of your life, firmly tied to all the rest.

The turn can start to demand a grand scale. Since a shake-up once opened up the world, you want to repeat it at full strength: not one pursuit changes but everything at once — friends, hobbies, routine, even the city. The first weeks make your head spin, as if fate were on your side again. But the parts of the new life don’t have time to grow together: acquaintances stay shallow, what you start never links up with the rest. When the excitement fades, what surrounds you is not a whole world but a heap of beginnings, and you are drawn to the next turn, just to feel movement again.

17-3-20.heading: Pour out inspiration and watch it take root in others
captions: The warmth of response and belonging
paragraphs: You feel good when you can express your vision with your hands: paint a cup, knit a pattern you saw in a dream, turn a sketch into a real thing. The Star pours the idea out generously, hiding nothing and holding nothing back. The Empress feeds the desire: you want something living to grow out of the sketch — something people use, something that brings joy every day. Judgement answers with warmth: when what you have made wakes joy in others and a wish to try it themselves, you feel among your own people.

**Your inspiration comes alive twice: when you create, and when others wake up in response.** Say you give a friend a cup you have painted, and a week later they bring you their first attempt and ask you to show them how it’s done. That is how a small circle of people who also wanted to make things gathers around a single pattern. What you made takes root beyond you, and there is a lot of warmth in that togetherness.

The response can turn into orders. “Make me one too”, “Can you get it done in time for the party?” — turning your own people down feels almost like betraying the very warmth that made you share. You agree, and the free pattern gives way to other people’s wishes, deadlines, identical mugs for every holiday. The idea you wanted to grow for yourself gets put off again and again. You are still among your own, but in your workshop there is more and more duty and less and less of the light that used to pour out by itself.

17-6-5.heading: Find a time-tested form for your feeling
captions: Beauty for someone you’re drawn to
The joy of a mastered form
paragraphs: Your ideas are almost always addressed to someone: you want to draw, sing or write something for a person you are drawn to. The Star makes your creativity open — the idea doesn’t hide but pours out generously, just as it is. The Lovers feed this desire: beauty gains meaning when you can share it with someone dear to you. And the Hierophant brings the satisfaction of a mastered form — the song is played as it should be, and you carry on the old custom of offering a feeling through art.

**Your feeling rings out in full once it has found its form.** Say you learn an old love song to sing it to one particular person. Weeks of practice give your hands confidence, and on the evening itself the familiar melody carries your voice: the words were written long ago, but the meaning in them is yours. The form keeps you from being swept away by the strength of the feeling, and afterwards a quiet pride remains: it came out both beautiful and honest.

A ready-made form can start speaking for you. Opening up directly is scarier than singing someone else’s lines, and more and more often your own awkward words give way to proven ones: a fitting love song, the right present for an anniversary, a card with a lovely quote. Everything is as it should be, and the other person is pleased. But showing yourself as you are, the very reason you wanted to create, never quite happens, and after the evening there is a vague sense that the wrong thing was said.

17-9-8.heading: A style of your own, found alone
captions: Letting your vision spill out freely
Wanting to find your own manner
paragraphs: A pencil, a guitar or a notebook is your way of letting your vision spill out without looking to anyone else’s example. The Star brings openness to these pursuits: you don’t hide what is clumsy, you let the idea flow as it is. What draws you, though, is not praise but your own understanding — the Hermit calls you to find your own manner and reach it by your own path. Afterwards Strength remains: the steady calm of someone who has nothing to prove in order to stay themselves.

**You arrive at your own manner by yourself, and that calms you more than any praise.** Say you have been drawing in the evenings for several years, and one day you notice that your line no longer looks like the lessons in your teach-yourself book: only you draw like this. There is more surprise in it than pride. And when someone asks how you got there, you gladly show them the way, without expecting them to follow in your exact footsteps.

Once you have found your voice, you want to keep it free of anything mixed in. Courses, other people’s sketchbooks, advice from the experienced start to feel like a threat: what if they teach you to draw “like everyone else” and your own manner dissolves? You steer clear of them and carry on alone. But without fresh water the stream runs shallow — the same techniques, the same subjects, each piece like the last. Calm confidence hardens into stubbornness, and enjoyment gives way to guarding your own style.

17-12-11.heading: Let an idea hang until it comes out true
captions: Releasing an idea in one sweep
A pause where you hear desire
paragraphs: Your ideas ripen in suspension: you lie listening to music, gaze out of the window, turn an idea this way and that, without doing anything about it yet. The Hanged Man feeds your desire with exactly this stillness — in it you can hear what you want to say, and a familiar story suddenly turns upside down. Then the Star pours what you have found out into the world, openly and generously: a sketch, a verse, a page. And Justice brings a special satisfaction: what you have made matches exactly what you lived through, with nothing extra and nothing prettified.

**You let an idea hang for a while, and that is why it comes out honest.** Say the whole evening goes on listening to the rain and writing nothing down. Then, closer to midnight, a drawing comes together in twenty minutes, and it holds exactly the mood you had been carrying inside. There is no need to explain or defend it. The time you gave yourself has come back as something real, and the exchange feels fair.

The pause can turn into a deal. If you have given up an evening, you want an idea in return — that’s only fair. You sit down to wait for inspiration the way you wait to be paid, counting the hours spent. But ideas don’t come on merit: sometimes after a week of silence, sometimes in a minute standing in a queue. An empty evening leaves resentment, as if your imagination had broken the contract, and the suspension turns from spellbound to tense — and under tension your view no longer turns upside down.

17-15-5.heading: A passion for material that grew into craft
captions: An almost physical pull to material
The satisfaction of a mastered craft
paragraphs: It all begins with an almost physical pull towards material: the smell of oil paint, the sound of a string, clay giving way under your fingers. The Devil makes this desire strong and tenacious — you don’t begrudge it your evenings or your money. The Star turns the pull into expression: you don’t just enjoy the material, you openly pour your vision into it. And the Hierophant then brings a master’s satisfaction: the passion has taken shape, and you understand a craft that generations have handed down to one another.

**Your passion for material knows how to grow into a craft.** Say watercolour grabs you one day, and for weeks you paint at night, unable to stop. At first the sheets are full of random blots, then understanding comes: how much water, when to wait, where to leave the white. The heat doesn’t cool, but now it has a channel, and every finished sheet says more about you than any words.

The pull can get stuck in the material itself. It is pleasant to spend hours mixing paints on the palette, admiring how colours shade into each other, trying out how each tint lies on the paper — the sensations come at once, with no effort. But the sheet stays blank: the vision that started it all finds no room. The evening passes in pleasure, yet afterwards there is neither a finished piece nor a sense that the craft has become any clearer, and contentment gives way to a stiffness, as if the time had gone on the wrong thing.

17-18-8.heading: Tame night-time images and share them
captions: Drawn to images from the half-dark
paragraphs: Your best work begins where you start to feel a little uneasy. The Moon stirs desire with images from the half-dark: a troubling dream, a strange melody, a late-evening mood that has no name. The Star gives these images a way out — you pour them generously into something: you write, sing, draw, without hiding behind anyone else’s style. And Strength answers afterwards: a calm confidence stays inside you, as if the wild thing that frightened you had become tame.

**For you, creating is a way to make friends with your own darkness.** Say a vague restlessness rolls in one evening. You could distract yourself, or you could sit down at your instrument or with a notebook and let it sound. An hour later it has a shape: a verse, a sketch, a few pages. The restlessness hasn’t gone, but it has become yours and no longer gives the orders. The pleasure here is born not of ease but of the courage to let everything that lives in you join the game.

You want to share it straight away, while the image is still hot. The late-night sketch goes off to a friend, the draft of a song to the group chat. But what came out of the half-dark hasn’t cooled yet and may seem unsettling to someone else. What comes back is silence or a careful “Are you all right?”, and you feel stripped bare in the cold. Then strength turns into restraint: the images stay with you, and the stream that used to bring joy slowly runs shallow.

17-21-11.heading: Pour your water into the common stream
captions: Wanting to join a larger whole
paragraphs: Your inspiration doesn’t stay inside — it needs to pour out. The Star shows up in pursuits where an idea can be given away openly: singing at a celebration, drawing a poster for friends, making a present with your own hands. The World calls you to keep going: you want your piece to go into something bigger — a festival, a shared album, a garden for the whole street. And Justice shapes the aftertaste: it feels good when what you give and what you get are in proportion.

**Your joy is to bring your own piece to the common whole and feel it land.** Say your neighbours decide to throw a party in the courtyard, and you take on the music. The evening is built by many hands: someone brought tables, someone brought pies, and the melody tied it all together. Everyone gave their share and got a shared evening back. The pleasure lies in the very way the exchange works: generosity isn’t wasted, because it goes into a whole that welcomes it.

The balance starts to slip when you want a response from the whole world at once. The wider the circle, the more you give: another post, another platform, another big project. But a big circle answers more quietly than a neighbour across a shared table: a handful of reactions to a piece that took a week. The scales tip, and every new thing begins with a quick reckoning of whether it will pay off in attention. The main thing drains out of the pursuit — the light that poured out simply because there was so much of it.

18-3-21.heading: Let what came at dusk take root
paragraphs: What is most alive in you is born in half-tones. The Moon leads you into pursuits where much stays unclear: late-night improvising without sheet music, music in the dark, a walk at dusk, writing down a dream before it melts away. The Empress explains why you want to come back: something begins to grow out of these wanderings — a motif, an image, an idea that needs time and care. And the World answers afterwards: life feels whole, as if night and day had joined into a single circle.

**For you, imagination is not an escape but soil.** Say that late in the evening you sit down at your instrument and let your hands wander. Month after month these wanderings sprout motifs you feel drawn back to; some you play for friends, others stay yours alone. There is no hurry: everything ripens at its own pace. And after evenings like these the world feels complete — even what troubled you in the daytime is in its place.

You want to protect that fullness, and so you start weeding everything unsettling out of your evening wanderings. A harsh chord seems superfluous, a sad motif out of place, a strange thought a weed. Only the soft and pretty is left, and for a while it looks like harmony. But the soil was fertile because light and murk were mixed in it. Without shadow the melodies turn smooth and alike: everything in the garden is tidy, only nothing new grows.

18-6-6.heading: Let someone close into your twilight
captions: Drawn to someone to share with
paragraphs: Your imagination comes alive when there is someone to share it with. The Moon shows up in the pursuits themselves: night walks, talking about dreams in the dark, reading aloud by candlelight. The Lovers play two roles here. In desire they stand for attraction and choice: you want to invite someone you are drawn to into this twilight. In the response they stand for openness: after an evening like that you are left feeling that you were with each other without masks.

**It brings you joy to let another person into your half-light and find that, together, it isn’t frightening there.** Say that late one evening you tell someone close to you about a strange dream, and they answer with one of their own. The hazy things that feel awkward to talk about by day become a shared secret instead of a shadow you carry alone. The pleasure here lies in trust: you are seen from an unfamiliar side, and the bond only grows stronger for it.

You want to protect that openness, and without noticing you start letting only the pretty part of the twilight in. A wistful dream, yes; a heavy mood can wait. Your loved one gets mysterious stories and subtle observations, while irritation and worry stay under a hard shell. The evenings are as magical as ever, but now it is a moonlit performance. The other person knows you by reflected light, your real shadow waits alone, and the feeling of closeness without masks gives way to weariness with your own role.

18-9-9.heading: Walk into the dark with your own lantern
captions: Wanting to figure it out yourself
A quiet light you can share
paragraphs: You are drawn to places where the familiar loses its sharp outlines: a sleeping city, night photography, a forest path at dusk, old legends at bedtime. That is how the Moon shows up in your pursuits. The Hermit plays two roles here. In desire he leads you along your own path: you want to make sense of what is unclear by yourself, without a guide or ready-made explanations. In the response he raises his lantern: what remains afterwards is a calm understanding that can light the way for someone else too.

**For you, darkness is not a threat but a place where your own light comes on.** Say you wander empty streets with a camera until your eyes adjust to the gloom. At first everything seems strange and a little unsettling, then details emerge that you never see by day: a streetlamp reflected in a puddle, a cat on a garage roof. You come home quiet and clear-headed, and your pictures help someone see a familiar city in a new way.

A light like this needs quiet, and quiet is easiest to find when everyone is asleep. Your walks move later and later, evening plans start to get in the way, invitations are turned down: the night is taken. The day feels noisy and foreign, and people seem too loud for what you have found. Friends stop asking. The lantern burns as before, but there is almost no one left to shine it for, and the quiet joy turns into a sense that you live in a different time zone from everyone you care about.

18-12-3.heading: Let the water guide the brush
captions: A sense that life bears fruit
paragraphs: You enjoy pursuits where the material lives a life of its own: watercolour on a wet sheet, ink spreading through water, music that guides your hands by itself. Here the Moon shows up as fluidity and half-tones: you never know in advance what will appear. The Hanged Man explains why you want to keep going: a spellbound pause sets in, in which you stop steering and simply watch, and the familiar turns to show another side. The Empress shapes the response — a feeling that life has more sap in it.

**Pleasure comes when you let the process lead you.** Say a patch of paint has spread the wrong way. You could blot it with a tissue, or you could stop and look: why, it’s mist over a river. You turn the sheet round, and the accident becomes the start of a landscape. You come out of evenings like these full, as if something had grown not only on the paper, and you want to share it — to give presents, to feed people, to invite them round.

Everything changes if you expect a harvest from every evening. You want to repeat a good sheet, and your hand starts directing the water: blot it here, touch it up there, keep the paint from running off over here. The work gets neater, but the spellbound pause you sat down for no longer comes — your attention is busy steering. A failed sheet now feels like a wasted evening. A living process turns into production, and instead of abundance there is worry: will it work out next time?

18-15-6.heading: A wild side free of shame
paragraphs: Night, music, dimmed lights — this is the setting in which you come alive. The Moon shows up in your pursuits: dancing in a half-dark hall, an open-air concert, a night drive to your favourite songs. The Devil explains the force of the desire: in the dark something physical and a little wild wakes up, and it is hard to stop — one more track, one more hour. And the Lovers decide what stays afterwards: tenderness, and the feeling that beside you was someone you didn’t need to hide anything from.

**Your wild side feels at home where it is shared without shame.** Say you dance with someone close to you deep into the night, forgetting how you look from the outside. The funny, the awkward, the passionate — it all fits, because you are both on the same wavelength. You go home tired and strangely light, as if you had shed a skin you no longer needed. Here attraction doesn’t destroy but draws you closer: lived through together, it becomes a shared secret.

Little by little, the openness gets tied to this spell. In daylight a direct conversation feels awkward, and important things are put off until evening, music and half-light, where everything will somehow get said by itself. The craving for atmosphere grows: without it, closeness never seems to switch on. Evenings become a condition rather than a joy — you need the right place, the right light, the right song. At night you are close, and in the morning you are polite again and a little like strangers, and what passed between you stays in the dark.

18-18-9.heading: Get to know your shadow in safe darkness
captions: Playing with the eerie and mysterious
paragraphs: You are drawn to what gives other people goosebumps: ghost stories, supernatural whodunnits, a scary tale by the campfire. The Moon plays two roles here. In your pursuits it offers the game with the shadow itself — a safe one that you can always step out of. In desire it becomes the call of the unknown: you are lured by what has not yet been explained, a path whose end you cannot see. The Hermit shapes the response — a quiet understanding of yourself that stays once the lights are back on.

**Fear within a safe frame helps you make out your own shadow.** Say that after a dark film you notice that what scared you was not the monster but the hero’s loneliness — and that tells you more about yourself than any test. This kind of knowledge isn’t read somewhere; you found it on your own. You come out of the darkness calmer than you went in, and you can support someone who is afraid: you know what this path looks like from the inside.

The swap happens when invented darkness becomes more comfortable than the real kind. In a story, fear arrives on schedule and ends on the last page, while in life the unclear drags on with no ending: an unanswered letter, perhaps, or a decision you don’t want to make. It is easier to open another dark story and live through the taming of terror. You learn more and more about fear, but your lantern shines only in invented corridors, while what troubles you right now stays off to one side.

18-21-12.heading: See your life in the great pattern of stories
captions: Wanting to see how everything connects
A pause that shifts your view
paragraphs: You are fascinated by what lives on the border between waking and dreaming: myths, folk tales from different peoples, dreams written down. That is how the Moon shows up in your pursuits. The World explains why you want to keep going: you look for how everything fits into one picture — the same story at opposite ends of the earth. The Hanged Man shapes the response: afterwards comes a spellbound pause in which your own life is seen from an unfamiliar angle.

**Ancient stories help you see your life as part of a larger pattern.** Say you read a tale about a descent into the underworld, and a week later you meet the same story in a song from another continent. The world seems bound together by invisible threads, and in that web there is a place for you. You sit still with the book on your knees, and a familiar difficulty looks like a passage that heroes of every age have gone through. It is not an answer but a different angle, and it makes things lighter.

The pattern can start to show through in too many places. If everything is connected, everyday coincidences look like messages too: a word you come across twice, a dream the night before, a number on a display board. You want to read them correctly, and decisions are put off until a clear sign appears. The pause that once turned your view around and brought release becomes waiting. The stories still enthral you, but they bring less and less relief: you freeze between signs, and your own wish never finds words.

19-3-22.heading: Sowing generously without knowing what will grow
captions: The lightness of an open ending
paragraphs: Your best times are sunny and a little childlike: a party in the courtyard, games on the grass, a shared vegetable plot where everyone plants whatever they like. The Sun makes your pastimes open and easy to invite others into. The Empress explains where the wish comes from: you want something to grow under your care and feed people — a vegetable bed, or a pie big enough for everyone. And the Fool shapes the aftertaste: lightness and curiosity, as if many roads lie ahead and you are bound to none of them.

**For you, joy is sowing generously and not knowing what will come up.** Say that in spring you and your friends scatter seeds with no plan at all: pumpkins next to nasturtiums, sunflowers along the fence. By summer you have a funny, motley garden where everything is jumbled up and everything is in flower. Nobody competes over who did more: you are glad of the harvest and of how easy it was to get it started. Here, pleasure needs no reasons.

Generosity can quietly eat up your own play. You want things to be easy for everyone, so you take on whatever holds the party together: feeding people, keeping the little ones busy, making sure nobody gets bored. Everyone around you feels warm and carefree. But you spend the whole day shining for others and never get your hands in the soil. By evening, instead of lightness, you feel a host’s weariness, and the curiosity that started it all has gone to the guests.

19-6-7.heading: Paddling in the same direction
paragraphs: You unwind best as a pair and out in the open: a two-person kayak, a bike ride along the river, partner dancing on an outdoor floor in summer. The Sun keeps these pastimes simple — no complicated goal, just play. The Lovers explain why you want more: you are drawn to someone you can share the movement with, and it matters that you chose this partner yourself. The Chariot sets the aftertaste — the thrill and pride of having got, together, to where you meant to go.

**You feel joy when two people pull in the same direction.** Say you are paddling out to a distant island: at first your paddles clash, the kayak goes round in circles and you laugh. Then you find a shared rhythm, and the boat runs smoothly, as if on its own. On the shore there is sunshine, tired shoulders and the feeling of a small shared victory. Play like this brings you closer than long talks do: you get to know each other in motion.

The thrill can take over the steering. You want to feel that surge again, so you take charge of course and pace: “left a bit”, “faster”, “come on, to the headland”. It looks like caring about success, but bit by bit your partner turns into a paddler working to orders, and the outing into a race against the clock. It is no longer much fun for them, and next time they may say they are busy. The island is reached, but the pull that put you both in one boat has been left behind at the start.

19-9-10.heading: Learning through play and enjoying every turn
paragraphs: You like learning through play — in the sun, with no exams: a skateboard or roller skates in an empty park, a kite, juggling on a lawn. The Sun keeps such pastimes simple: there is no shame in falling, and laughing is allowed. The Hermit explains where the wish comes from: you want to work things out for yourself, at your own pace, without a coach or comparisons. And the Wheel of Fortune decides what stays with you afterwards: the buzz of seeing everything on the move — yesterday it would not work, today it suddenly clicks.

**You can enjoy both the fall and the rise, because you see them as one circle.** Say that for a week the board keeps shooting out from under your feet, and then one morning you ride the whole length of the path. A couple of days later you fail again — and now it does not scare you: after a dip comes the next turn. There is a calm in this kind of play, right in the middle of the movement. You are not chasing results, yet the skill grows, because you stay in the game.

You want to keep the lightness, so you steer clear of anything that might disturb it. The familiar works, while the next step — the first ride down a slope, a jump, going where others are watching — is a little frightening. It seems its time has not come yet. You ride along the same path, and every morning looks like the one before. There are no more turns, and the buzz gives way to boredom, though a new cycle was just one clumsy step away.

19-12-4.heading: Giving yourself a day off and seeing home anew
captions: Wanting to stop and look again
The calm of owning your time
paragraphs: You love sunny days with nothing to get done: a hammock in the garden, badminton on the lawn, lunch on the grass. The Sun keeps this kind of rest simple. The Hanged Man explains where the wish comes from: you want to drop out of the rush and see the familiar from another side — to hang your head over the side of the hammock and see the garden upside down. The Emperor sets the aftertaste: a calm certainty that your time is yours to command, and that today you have chosen to give it to yourself.

**You feel good when a holiday of doing nothing is your own firm decision.** Say that on Friday you announce: Saturday is for doing nothing. A morning in the hammock, a lazy shuttlecock over the net, tea until noon. At some point you look at the house from the lawn and see not a list of repairs but a place where life is good. By evening there is a steady certainty inside: this is your life, and you are the one in charge of it, not the hired help.

Your pause can start charging an entry fee: first get everything in order, then rest. The sunny Saturday will have to wait while the windows are unwashed, the papers unsorted and the grass uncut. The rule sounds sensible, and you keep to it strictly. But order in a household is never final: behind one job you can already see the next. The pause is pushed back to the evening, then to another weekend. Your time is still yours to command — there is just hardly any holiday left in it.

19-15-7.heading: Playing your heart out until sundown
captions: Games in the sun, with company
A gripping urge to play on
paragraphs: You are drawn to games in the sun and in company: beach volleyball, a kickabout in the courtyard, tennis in the park, relay races at a summer fête. The Sun makes them open and simple — anyone can be called in, and the rules take a minute to learn. The Devil explains the strength of the wish: the game grips your body and your competitive streak, and it is hard to tear yourself away — one more game, one more set, while you can still see the ball. The Chariot shapes the aftertaste: triumph when you win a point, a game, and sometimes the whole tournament.

**You love giving a game everything you have and feeling the whole group catch fire along with you.** Say that towards evening an impromptu tournament forms on the beach: the teams are all mixed up, the score is kept with a stick in the sand, and supporters shout from their towels. You race about until the last ball, and the win, however much of a joke, rings inside you all evening. There is no malice in this kind of competitive fire: it makes the day brighter for everyone around you.

The chain tightens when you cannot leave without a win. A lost set demands a rematch, the rematch another one, the sun is already going down, and you keep calling out: “last one, the decider”. The others have long wanted a swim but give way to your push. The game stops being a celebration and becomes a debt you have to win back. Even a victory after an evening like that brings relief rather than triumph, and next time the group may gather in the meadow without you.

19-18-10.heading: Staging a fairy tale in broad daylight
captions: A pull towards mystery and make-believe
The buzz of an unexpected twist
paragraphs: For you, a party works when there is a little magic in it. The Sun makes your free time open and simple: a game on the grass, a shared bonfire, some scheme that children and grown-ups alike are invited to join. The Moon feeds your interest in mystery — you want riddles, dressing up, stories where not everything is clear at once. And the Wheel of Fortune brings a lift afterwards: the day turned away from where it was heading, and something happened that nobody expected that morning.

**In your hands an ordinary day easily turns into a fairy tale anyone can step into.** Say that at a birthday party at a country cottage you hide notes with riddles all over the garden, and by evening the grown-ups are running about just like the children. Nobody knows where the next clue will lead, and that is the best part. When the treasure turns up under the old apple tree, everyone is left with the feeling that life knows how to surprise you, if only you give it a little help.

To keep the surprise, you want the whole scheme to stay secret. You prepare it alone, wave away offers of help and get upset if someone guesses too soon. The magic works, but the party looks more and more like your own show, with everyone else in the audience. The shared game, where anyone could have turned the story their own way, never quite happens, and what remains afterwards is not a lift but the weariness of a magician who worked without assistants.

19-21-4.heading: Bringing everyone into one game
captions: The calm of a well-ordered day
paragraphs: For you, a game becomes real when everyone is drawn into it. The Sun keeps your free time simple and open: rounders in a meadow, a shared lunch under the trees, songs that everyone knows. The World gives you the wish to gather different things into one whole — children and adults, old friends and new neighbours — so that nobody is left on the sidelines. And the Emperor brings a calm certainty afterwards: the day was well put together, and the party had a beginning, a middle and a good ending.

**With you, a crowd of very different people comes together as one cheerful circle.** Say that at the country cottage you start a game of skittles that has a part for everyone, from a seven-year-old to the elderly neighbour. Some throw, some keep score, some cheer. By evening everyone is sitting at one table, and there is solid ground underfoot: here is a place where everyone is happy and everything is where it should be.

It stings when anyone steps outside the circle. If someone would rather stay in the hammock with a book, or has started a game of their own in a corner of the garden, the picture feels incomplete, and you call them again and again until they give in. Order is restored and everyone is together, but now the game includes someone who takes no joy in it. The party holds firm, yet the lightness drains out of it: what keeps it whole is your effort, not what each person wants.

20-3-5.heading: Passing on a skill and letting it grow
captions: Waking a skill in someone else
Wanting what you sow to sprout
Part of a chain of masters
paragraphs: You want not only to keep a skill you love but to awaken it in others. Judgement here is the very moment of response: you call, and someone convinced they are “all fingers and thumbs” suddenly lights up. The Empress feeds the wish to make things grow: let what you have sown sprout and bear fruit, even in someone else’s hands. And the Hierophant brings a quiet satisfaction afterwards — as you explain, you understand the craft more deeply yourself and feel like a link in the chain of people who handed it down before you.

**Your skill truly comes alive when it wakes up in someone else.** Say you are teaching a friend to bake sourdough bread. Her first loaf comes out lopsided, the second dense, and after the fifth she sends you a photo with three exclamation marks. Her joy feels like a continuation of yours. And in answering her questions, you put into words for the first time why the dough behaves exactly as it does.

Yet what you sow grows in its own way. Your pupil starts adding things to the bread that you would never put in, changes the timings, finds another mentor — and a jealous “that’s not how it’s done” rises inside you. You want to bring her back into line, so you correct, remind, get upset. But the awakening you once sparked was her own, and it leads further than your school. If you cling to the proper way, it is easy to lose the main joy — seeing the skill alive.

20-6-8.heading: Reawakening an old friendship
captions: Bringing the dormant back to life
paragraphs: Get-togethers that wake what has dozed off bring you a special joy. Judgement gives your free time the taste of coming back to life: gathering old friends for a hike as you did many years ago, digging out forgotten board games, calling everyone round for songs with a guitar. The Lovers draw you to this — a pull towards people you once felt warm with. What remains afterwards is Strength: old grudges lose their weight, and you feel calmer and gentler than before you met.

**Around you, people who have drifted apart come alive to each other again.** Say you talk your old university classmates into spending a weekend by a lake. The first half hour is awkward, then someone remembers an old joke, and everyone seems to wake up. By the campfire that evening, people who have not phoned each other for years are arguing and laughing again.

You want what you have woken to be just as it was. You expect the same jokes, the same roles, the same talk until dawn, but people have changed: one has worries you know nothing about, another goes to bed first. Every mismatch with your memories grates, and you try to bring back “the way it used to be”. After a reunion like that, instead of a warm strength you are left with frustration, and the people as they are now, the ones you reached out to, remain almost strangers.

20-12-5.heading: Returning to the forgotten and rediscovering it
captions: A pause where the wish speaks
paragraphs: Sometimes real pleasure comes not from something new but from something put aside long ago: an instrument from childhood, abandoned paints, a dance you have not gone back to for years. In your pastimes Judgement is the answer to such a call: an old interest rises, as if someone had spoken its name. The Hanged Man explains where the wish comes from: you hear it when you stop, when the rush lets go and the familiar can be seen from another side. The Hierophant shapes the aftertaste — the joy of a craft understood and the sense of having entered a long tradition.

**For you, pleasure is reclaiming what was once yours and seeing it with new eyes.** Say that after a long break you sit down at the piano again. Your fingers remember less, but your ear has changed: now you understand why your teacher insisted on playing slowly, and the piece sounds deeper. The return does not repeat the past but carries it on, and after the evening you are left with a certainty: your interest has roots.

Bitterness creeps in when the return turns into a trial of the missed years. You want to prove the interest was genuine, so you hold yourself to a strict standard: how people who never gave up play, what the syllabus says you should be able to do. Every mistake sounds like a verdict on leaving all those years ago. The pause that gave birth to the wish gives way to a rush to catch up, and all that is left of the joy of rediscovery is an exam in which you are your own examiner.

20-15-8.heading: Coming alive in every limb and staying yourself
paragraphs: You come alive through whatever lifts both body and mood: a concert where the whole hall is on its feet at the first chords, dancing until dawn, a big open-air celebration. In such pastimes Judgement is an awakening: a call sounds, and everything that was dozing rises in answer. The Devil explains why you are drawn back: the sensations hold on tight, and they are hard to give up. Strength accounts for what remains afterwards — the feeling that the passion was lived to the full and still did not carry you off.

**For you, a strong pull can become an awakening rather than a tether.** Say that after a night of dancing the morning feels brand new: your body is humming, your head is clear, yesterday’s worries are behind you. You gave yourself to the music completely, but the choice to leave or stay was yours all along. From experiences like this grows a gentle command of yourself: not a ban, but the knack of steering your impulse without breaking it.

Confidence in your own strength can start demanding proof. You want to feel again that you are in control of the impulse, so you deliberately move closer to it: one more night “just to see”, one more test that you will stop whenever you choose. Each line you hold makes you proud, but your attention is taken up more and more by the pull itself. The celebration turns into a trial, and the awakening never comes: it is hard to wake up when you spend the whole evening keeping watch over yourself.

20-18-11.heading: Giving the forgotten back its place
captions: Bringing the forgotten back to life
paragraphs: You are drawn to what lies in the shadows waiting to be noticed: old letters from a flea market, the overgrown garden of an abandoned manor, recordings by a performer nobody has listened to for years. In your pastimes Judgement shows up as revival: the forgotten rises and is heard again. The wish is stirred by the Moon — the call of half-light, of a story half told, with more questions than answers. And Justice decides what remains afterwards: the satisfaction that a thing or a name has finally found the place it deserves.

**What delights you is leading something unfairly forgotten out of the twilight.** Say a box of old snapshots turns up a photograph with an inscription, and you spend weeks finding out who is in it. Your imagination suggests theories, your finds test them, and little by little the stranger’s face acquires a name and a story. When you show it to others, you feel at peace inside: the world is a little fairer than it was before your discovery.

It is easy to go astray when a guess starts to feel final. In twilight the light is only reflected, and the story comes together too neatly: the forgotten author must have been hounded, the abandoned house was surely taken unjustly. You want everyone to get their due, and the verdict is passed before the facts are in. A new find that does not fit now irritates rather than delights. Instead of a living search, all that is left is defending your version, and what you wanted to bring out of the shadows ends up with an invented fate instead of its real one.

20-21-5.heading: Closing the circle and stepping up a level
captions: Moving up to a new level
Wanting to walk the whole path
paragraphs: Your pleasure often ripens towards a moment of transition: a grading at your club, an end-of-year concert, your first time on stage. Judgement shows up in exactly these milestones — you leave the old level behind and answer the call of the new one. The World feeds the wish: you want to walk the whole path, to master every side of the craft rather than grab a convenient piece of it. The Hierophant decides what remains afterwards — a sense of belonging to a school and to those who walked this path before you.

**A full circle, completed and recognised, delights you more than any single success.** Years at a dance school can come together in one performance where everything meets: technique, music, partner, stage. Afterwards your teacher shakes your hand, and it is not a formality but a sign that the craft has been handed on. A milestone like this does not end your interest — it shows that you have become part of something bigger than your own hobby.

The circle can close too tightly. You have walked the path, the school knows and respects you, yet inside the call sounds again — to try something else, to start from scratch. But somewhere new you would be a beginner, while here you have a name and a seat in the front row. So you stay: you go to the same classes, keep the usual order going, help the younger ones. The belonging remains, but the awakening that once brought you into this hall grows ever fainter.

21-3-6.heading: Bringing home things that can grow
captions: Wanting to grow what you saw
paragraphs: Your interest wakes up on the road: an unfamiliar city, a market in a foreign country, a workshop where clay or wool is worked in its own way. The World shows in how you spend your time — through a breadth of impressions and getting to know other ways of living and making things. The Empress explains what draws you further: you want not just to see but to bring home something alive — seeds, a sourdough starter, a technique from which something of your own will grow. And the Lovers shape the aftertaste: tenderness towards the place and the people who shared what was theirs with you.

**For you, a trip goes on for as long as what you brought back keeps growing.** Tomatoes grown from seeds bought at a mountain market may turn red on your balcony a year later, and a bread recipe from a village bakery may become your Sunday loaf. Each such fruit is a small continuation of the encounter. You share it with your loved ones, tell them where it comes from, and the warmth of that place becomes something you all hold in common.

Things go wrong when what you brought back has to please everyone. You want your loved ones to love it as much as you do, so little by little you adjust: you leave out the hot spices, simplify the pattern, tell the story of the trip more briefly so as not to bore anyone. Every polite “well, not bad” makes you change something else. In time the dish becomes familiar to everyone, but the flavour you fell in love with is gone, and the joy of your own discovery now hangs on other people’s opinion.

21-6-9.heading: Making something whole for someone you love
captions: Making it for a loved one
paragraphs: You love big projects made up of many parts: a family album, a patchwork quilt, a handwritten recipe book. The World shows in your drive to bring the work to completeness, where every part has its own place. The Lovers explain where the wish comes from: you want to make such a thing for someone you are drawn to, and to put beauty into it. The Hermit decides what remains afterwards — a quiet understanding: over months of work it becomes clear why this person is so dear to you.

**In making something for a loved one, you also find out what they mean to you.** As you match patch to patch or photo to photo, conversations and small things you had long stopped thinking about come back to you. You work alone, yet the other person seems to be beside you the whole time. When the piece is finished, you can hand it over — and with it, the understanding you have reached.

The whole may never arrive. You want the gift to be worthy of the feeling, and something more keeps asking to go in: a new photo, one more recipe, a different shade of fabric. The work goes on in secret so as not to spoil the surprise, and nobody is there to say “it’s already lovely”. Months turn into years, the relationship lives its own life, and the almost-finished piece waits on a shelf. The understanding that could have been shared stays with you alone.

21-9-3.heading: From grain all the way to the shared table
captions: The urge to work it out
paragraphs: You like following a thing’s whole journey: from grain to loaf, from milk to a matured cheese, from the hive to a jar of honey on the shelf. The World shows in your wish to take in the work completely, with all its stages and seasons. The Hermit explains what keeps the interest alive: you want to work things out yourself, unhurriedly, through your own trials. The Empress shapes the aftertaste — the joy of living abundance, when what you put in has ripened and there is more than enough of it.

**Something made from start to finish has a special taste for you.** Your first home-made cheese may not come out perfect, but you understand why it is the way it is: what the weather was like, how long it was left, where you went wrong. That knowledge makes the pleasure deeper. And when the harvest grows plentiful, you want to share it: give some to the neighbours, take a jar round to friends, lay a table with your own produce.

Generosity starts to taste bitter when there is an invisible journey behind it. You know how many months and attempts went into a single jar of honey, but to a guest it is just honey — nice, but ordinary. You want them to grasp what it cost, so you start telling the story, explaining, waiting for some special word. When it does not come, resentment rises inside. The quiet exploring that was yours alone turns into a bill presented to others, and the living process no longer brings joy for its own sake.

21-12-6.heading: Seeing your home through a guest’s eyes
paragraphs: Foreign countries can come to you on their own: guests from abroad on your sofa, a language club on Fridays, a festival that brings people to town from everywhere. In this kind of free time the World shows up as different lives meeting in one place. The wish is fed by the Hanged Man: it is fascinating to see the familiar turned upside down — through someone else’s eyes, from an unusual angle. And the Lovers decide what remains afterwards — the warmth of mutual liking, as if in a few days you have managed to become close.

**Through a guest, you get to know your own life all over again.** You might show a visitor around your neighbourhood — and they will stop dead at a peeling wall you had long since ceased to notice, or laugh at something you have always taken for granted. The everyday suddenly looks astonishing, and you seem more interesting than you thought you were. Encounters like these leave you with tenderness both for people and for the place where you live.

Goodbyes can cost too much. In three days you manage to grow attached, learn someone’s habits and share your own, and then they leave and the flat feels empty. To keep it from hurting, next time you want to hold back a little: show them the city, feed them, but not open up. There are still plenty of guests, only the tenderness no longer comes, and the wonder at the familiar, the very reason you invited people, fades along with it.

21-15-9.heading: Assembling the full picture and knowing its worth
paragraphs: Your interest often takes the form of collecting: records from a single label across all its years, minerals from different continents, old maps that together show a whole era. The World shows in the drive for completeness — for every item to find its place in the bigger picture. The Devil explains the strength of the wish: the hunt for the next find holds you tight, and the thought of a missing piece is hard to let go. And the Hermit decides what remains afterwards — a connoisseur’s quiet knowledge, which came not from a catalogue but from your own long search.

**For you, a strong pull becomes a road to real understanding.** Years of searching teach you to tell the rare from the merely old, to hear the difference between editions, to see a story in a scratch on a spine. Knowledge like that cannot be bought along with the object. You want to light the way for others with it: tell a newcomer where to look, show what makes this particular piece special, and be glad when someone’s eyes start to shine.

The thrill of the hunt can demand that you keep your light under your cloak. If others hear about a rare find, they might snap it up first, so you start keeping quiet: you do not name places, you answer evasively, you keep information to yourself. Fellow collectors who used to be good company turn into rivals. The collection grows and the knowledge deepens, but sharing it feels more and more frightening. The connoisseur’s quiet joy gives way to wariness, and instead of a lantern for others you are left with a treasure house that has to be guarded.

21-18-12.heading: Suspended between sky and water
captions: The call of water at night
paragraphs: You love long journeys that make a circle: sailing round an island, kayaking a ring of lakes, coming back to where you started. In this kind of free time the World shows up as a journey made whole — everything has been covered, and the start has met the end. The Moon explains what calls you: water at night, reflected light, a shore that loses its outline at dusk. And the Hanged Man decides what remains afterwards — a sense of suspension, when time seems to stand still and everyday worries are seen from the other side.

**In hours like these you drop out of life’s usual course and come back seeing things differently.** The boat may rest on the night water so still that the stars are reflected beneath you and you can no longer tell which way is up. You can lie there and watch, deciding nothing. By morning the urgent has shrunk and the important has become clear. The closed circle gives a sense of completion, and that makes it easy to go home.

Night water enchants, but it also unsettles. Along with the silence comes fear of the unknown: what is out there in the dark, will you make it back to shore in time. You want to feel that weightlessness without the unease, so bit by bit the routes become familiar, the forecasts flawless, the campsites tried and tested. There is less fear, but the stillness you set out for goes too. It lived at the edge of the known, and in a safe bay the circle is completed smoothly — only time no longer stops.

21-21-6.heading: Bringing together everything you love
captions: Wanting to weave it all together
paragraphs: You are drawn to trying life from different sides: one weekend the potter’s wheel, the next the climbing wall, a choir in spring, a hike in summer. In your pastimes the World gives you this breadth of experience. In the wish it works differently: you want to keep going when the different strands start to connect, and the breathing you learned in the choir suddenly helps you on a steep climb. The Lovers decide what remains afterwards — a love of life and of the people you have met along these roads.

**You see threads between things that seem incompatible to others.** From a hike you might bring a campfire song back to the choir, and from the pottery class a present for a friend from the climbing wall. This is how your hobbies weave into one fabric with room for many people. What delights you is not the number of pastimes but the way they echo each other — and the fact that around you people meet who would never have met otherwise.

You want all your circles to love each other as much as you love them. At a shared party the choir singers, the climbers and your old friends stand about in separate huddles, and you spend the whole evening translating between them, tossing in topics they have in common, checking that everyone is all right. The conversations stay polite, but the spark you were hoping for never flares up. You go home a tired go-between: there were plenty of dear people around you, yet you never really got to be with any one of them.

22-3-7.heading: Start with no experience, reap a harvest
captions: A bold try with no experience
The thrill of the first push
paragraphs: You like taking on things you can’t do yet: laying out a vegetable patch from a video, getting a sourdough starter going by guesswork, sitting down at a potter’s wheel for the first time. The Fool shows up in this ease — you can have a go without knowing how it will end, and without being afraid of mistakes. The Empress explains what calls you to keep going: you want the attempt to grow into something living and generous that truly bears fruit. And the Chariot shapes what stays with you afterwards — the thrill of momentum and the feeling of a small victory: it worked, and you were the one who made it work.

**You can start with no certainty at all and see a first attempt through to the harvest.** The first courgettes from a bed you planted on a hunch delight you more than shop-bought ones, because there’s courage behind them. Each result like this nudges you further: the unfamiliar gives way once you step into it. The thrill doesn’t die out at the start line but finds something to lean on in what is growing.

A carefree start can leave you with cares nobody thought about. You want to feel that first push again, and the projects multiply: one more bed, another sourdough starter, a bucket of clay on the balcony. Suddenly there’s more harvest than you have the energy to manage: courgettes pile up by the crate, the dough turns sour, and you can’t move in the kitchen for flour. The victory is still there, but irritation creeps into it, and the abundance it all began for goes to waste before it has a chance to bring you any joy.

22-6-10.heading: Step out unscripted to meet a partner
captions: Onto the stage without a script
The pull of a live partner
The sense of a lucky turn
paragraphs: You enjoy pastimes you can’t prepare for in advance: improv theatre, a jam session, dancing with a stranger on an open-air dance floor. The Fool shows up in this step into the unknown — you walk out without knowing what will happen, and the edge holds no fear for you. The Lovers explain what keeps you interested: the pull towards the real person facing you, the wish to hear them and to answer. And the Wheel of Fortune shapes the afterglow — the feeling that the story turned of its own accord and luck was on your side.

**Your best moments come when two people have no idea where things will carry them.** Your partner might throw out an unexpected line — you pick it up, and the story heads off somewhere nobody planned. The audience laughs, and you feel it could only have happened together. Turns like these leave a sense that life is fluid and generous with surprises, as long as you meet them openly.

After evenings like these, ordinary life can feel too flat. A quiet dinner with someone close to you, where nothing happens, starts to wear on you, and without meaning to you throw in twists: a spontaneous trip, a sudden change of plans, a question that knocks them off balance. They just want to be near you, and once again they’re being called onto the stage. They grow tired and answer with more and more reserve, and the novelty you were after arrives without the main thing — the attraction that grows in calm.

22-9-4.heading: Travel light and stand on your own feet
captions: The road with just a rucksack
The pull of your own path
paragraphs: You’re drawn to setting off light: a rucksack on your back, a local train to a station you don’t know, a day that takes shape along the way. The Fool shows up in this easy step — worldly trifles have little hold on you, and the unknown round the bend doesn’t frighten you. The Hermit explains the pull: you want to walk your own path, light the way with your own lantern and make sense of what you see without a tour guide. The Emperor shapes what stays afterwards — a calm steadiness: you know you can rely on yourself.

**The less you take with you, the surer of yourself you feel.** Perhaps by the very first evening it becomes clear how little a good day needs: water, a warm jacket, a trail and your own wits. A trip like this gives back a sense of footing that doesn’t depend on things or on other people’s decisions. You come home collected, and everyday tasks feel manageable.

Lightness can turn into a rulebook. You want to feel in command of yourself again, and the rules appear: no more than seven kilos, no souvenirs, no detours from the route that you haven’t approved in advance. A pleasant surprise — a fellow traveller with a thermos, an invitation to dinner, an extra day by the sea — now irritates you, because it breaks the order. The trips become flawless, but the Fool in them no longer steps towards the edge: he walks by instructions he wrote for himself.

22-12-7.heading: Find your way by trying
captions: Hang still, see what you want
paragraphs: An unfamiliar pastime pulls at you more than a familiar one: a surfboard, tap dancing, an oil sketch. The Fool gives these attempts their lightness — you’re allowed to fall and laugh at yourself. The Hanged Man feeds the desire with a particular kind of pause: in the middle of the attempt, time seems to hang still, your usual view turns upside down, and it becomes clear what you really want. And the Chariot brings excitement and triumph afterwards: you’ve moved from where you stood, and the direction was your own choice.

**You find your way by trying, not by planning.** Say you’re standing up on a board for the first time. You spend most of the morning falling off, and between waves you lie on the water and gaze at the shore, which seems quite different from out here. In that quiet it’s clear: you want more. And when you finally manage to ride a few metres, the joy is as if you had been commanding the sea yourself.

The attempt goes sour when doubters turn up behind you. “Why do you even need this?”, “It’s not for you” — and an easy pastime turns into a debate. Now the point is not to try but to prove: every wave becomes evidence, every fall a point for those who didn’t believe in you. The right to make mistakes is gone, the pauses on the water are spent answering critics in your head, and victory brings not a thrill but a grim “Well, convinced now?” Over all this arguing, you can no longer hear whether you actually want it yourself.

22-15-10.heading: Give in to temptation as if playing
captions: The sense of a lucky turn
paragraphs: The temptation to try things has a strong hold on you: an unfamiliar cuisine, dancing till dawn in a strange city, a fairground ride that takes your breath away. The Devil makes no secret of how strong this pull is — it’s physical, tenacious, hard to put off. The Fool makes the trying light: you step into the unknown with no plan and no fear of looking clumsy. And the Wheel of Fortune brings a buzz afterwards — life has taken a turn, and you were lucky enough to be in the right place.

**For you, giving in to temptation is a game, not a verdict.** Say you’re in a city you don’t know and you step into a cellar bar with music drifting out, and an hour later you’re dancing with people you hadn’t met that morning. Nobody planned anything, and it all came together. Next morning you’re left with a cheerful surprise: so that’s the turn an ordinary evening can take.

A lucky try easily becomes a habit that still calls itself freedom. You liked that cellar bar — and now you go there every Friday, order the same thing, dance with the same people. The pull remembers the taste and leads you down a familiar route, while you still think of it as spontaneity. Only there are no more turns: the buzz has given way to boredom, and it’s hard to give up, because it’s “just for fun”.

22-18-4.heading: Play someone else, return as yourself
captions: A pull towards masks and mystery
paragraphs: Becoming someone else for a little while is one of the pleasures that draws you most. The Fool makes these experiments light: a costume at a masquerade, a character in a role-playing game, someone else’s walk — with no demand to be good at it straight away and no fear of looking silly. The Moon feeds your interest with mystery: in a mask, by candlelight, in an invented world, sides of you surface that have no place on an ordinary day. And the Emperor brings calm afterwards: you return to your own life and feel you’re standing firmly in it.

**Having been someone else, you become more confidently yourself.** Say you spend a role-playing weekend living for two days as a gruff captain. You can say what you usually keep to yourself and try on a daring you’re not used to. On Monday you’re back among your own tasks and rules, and they feel like support rather than a cage: you know who you are because you’ve seen your other faces too.

It gets unsettling when make-believe starts seeping into everyday life. The captain’s daring might burst out in a meeting, a strange thought from the game might not let go all evening, and the order your calm rests on seems to crack. You want to draw the line more firmly, and then to give up games altogether: they stir you up too much. Your footing is restored, but the lightness leaves along with the masks, and the sides of you that were never accepted keep up a muffled knocking from within.

22-21-7.heading: Experience the world in every element
captions: A light step into the unknown
Wanting to feel the whole world
paragraphs: You want to experience the world in all its elements: water that holds you up, wind that lifts you, earth underfoot on a long climb, a fire you’ve lit with your own hands. The World feeds this desire — to feel life whole, not just one side of it. The Fool makes the trying light: you take on the unfamiliar without preparation and without fear of looking like a beginner. And the Chariot brings a thrill afterwards: you’re in motion, and the world answers every step you take.

**Each new element adds to your sense that the world is open.** Say that in a single summer you raft down a river for the first time, take off on a paraglider with an instructor and learn to light a fire in the rain. You haven’t mastered any of it, but your body remembers how water holds you and how the wind catches you. The world has come closer, and you truly live in it.

The elements can start to look like rivals. The river must be conquered, the mountain taken, the wind outwitted, and every attempt turns into a duel where what matters is coming out on top. The thrill grows, the trophies pile up, but it’s hard to feel kinship with something you’re at war with. You come back victorious but without the quiet delight you went for: the world you wanted to embrace whole has turned into a string of opponents.

5-15-20.heading: A feast by custom and a sense of renewal
paragraphs: You find it easier to give strong desires free rein where they have a recognised place: a family feast kept the old way, a carnival, Shrovetide fairs, a party with singing until dawn. The Hierophant shows in this respect for custom — pleasure is written into tradition and so needs no excuses. The Devil feeds the thirst itself: for the delicious, the loud, the bodily, for anything that carries you away completely. And Judgement decides what remains afterwards — a sense of awakening, as if a trumpet had sounded inside you and you had woken up renewed.

**Tradition gives your thirst for life its banks, and after the high water comes renewal.** The celebration is lived to the full, and then a clear morning arrives: you want to tidy up, start something new, see ordinary days differently. That is when a lot becomes clear — what mattered, who is truly dear to you, what it is time to give up. Here pleasure does not argue with meaning; it leads you to it.

Custom can start wanting things for you. It is what people do: one more toast, one more dish, stay to the very end, move on with everyone to the next place. Your own desire was satisfied long ago, but saying no would mean dropping out of the shared celebration, and the pull of the crowd holds tighter than any personal passion. In the morning the awakening comes all the same, only instead of renewal it brings a clear and unpleasant conclusion: most of the evening was not yours.

7-9-16.heading: Your own summit and an honest look at it
captions: Wanting to get there your way
A jolt that makes things clearer
paragraphs: For you, pleasure comes from a challenge you have chosen yourself. The Chariot shows in pursuits that test you: a solo hike, a difficult piece on an instrument, a trail you want to finish without a single stop. The Hermit explains the motive: what draws you is not competition but your own path to a height where you truly understand the thing. The Tower adds a jolt to what you feel afterwards — after the effort, your old confidence in your skill cracks, and you can see how things really stand.

**Your passion stays alive as long as it is willing to show you the truth.** You finish a route and realise you prepared for the wrong thing; you work through a piece and hear that your old technique was held together by habit. In the moment it is unpleasant, but discoveries like these lead to the next turn of the spiral: the old support gives way, and you build a new, sturdier one. The joy is a grown-up one — the joy of having become stronger not in your imagination but in fact.

What gets in the way is the habit of going it alone right to the end. You want to get there your own way, so advice and other people’s eyes seem unnecessary, and doubts are settled with one more push. Small errors pile up unnoticed, and the truth arrives all at once — in a single failure after which the whole pursuit seems to have collapsed. Instead of steady growth you get a seesaw: a long, stubborn climb, a sudden fall, the urge to quit. The pleasure of the journey gives way to fear of the next crash.

7-21-10.heading: A road after which life takes a turn
captions: A pull towards the whole world
The feeling of a new cycle
paragraphs: You feel most alive on a road you map out yourself. The Chariot shows in holidays that are journeys: a road trip, a long cycling tour, backpacking from town to town. The World explains the call: you want to take in more — a change of scenery, language and food, all your impressions joined into one big picture. The Wheel of Fortune colours what remains afterwards — the feeling that life has come full circle and brought you home, but on a new turn of the spiral.

**In motion you find a steadiness your usual routine does not always give you.** While towns and weather change, things grow calm inside: everything takes its course, and you move along with it. Each trip becomes a chapter of its own, and like the rings of a tree they show how you have changed. You come back with a fresh view of everyday things and plenty of strength in reserve for them.

The catch is that you start expecting the turn to come only from the road. It seems that life changes only out there, on the move, while at home everything stands still. An ordinary week becomes a waiting room: you scroll through routes, count the days, put joy off until the next trip. Back home, you soon feel stuck and start planning your escape again. The trips multiply, yet the sense that life has really moved on comes less and less often: between journeys you barely live it.

8-15-5.heading: Enjoying what you love
paragraphs: In Svadhisthana, the chakra linked with water, desire, sensuality and a taste for life come alive. Strength helps you treat attraction with care: acknowledge it and choose how to follow it. The Devil shows how easily what is pleasant starts dictating terms — you want more even when there is hardly any pleasure left. The Hierophant adds an inner verdict: after the experience, it matters to you to feel that you have stayed true to yourself.

Here pleasure becomes complete when you neither have to earn it nor justify it. You can get absorbed in creative work, give yourself to intimacy, spend a day on something you love — and feel that this is good, and that it is enough. **You can want something badly and still choose.** That is the gentleness of Strength: desire gets its place in your life, and with it you keep the freedom to stop, change your mind, save something for later.

The most exhausting trap is to forbid yourself too much at first and then make up for it all at once. Your inner judge demands self-control, desire builds up, and one day you want to throw every limit to the wind. Brief relief is followed by guilt. Pleasure loses its taste because almost all your attention goes on the struggle: hold back, give in, pull yourself together again.

10-12-22.heading: Accepting twists and travelling light
paragraphs: Your free time often goes off plan, and that is its charm. The Wheel of Fortune shows how your interest plays out: the weather, a chance meeting, a cancelled train change the weekend, and you turn along with them. The Hanged Man explains where desire comes from: in a forced pause you go still, look at the familiar upside down, and suddenly notice what you really want. The Fool is in charge of the aftertaste — lightness and curiosity, as if an open road lies ahead.

**You meet a plan falling through with interest, not irritation.** The train is three hours late — and you get a walk round an unfamiliar little town. Rain cancels the picnic — and an evening over a board game stays with you more vividly than the plan would have. You can wait out a turn without fuss and then step into something new with interest, without asking it for any promises. That is why your pleasure rarely depends on perfect conditions.

Over time you can get used to chance always making the choice. Putting your own wish into words seems almost unnecessary: circumstances will turn, something will come up. The pause drags on, and you stay in it while others invite, suggest, decide. The lightness remains, but looks more and more like absent-mindedness: you seem free, yet you have not taken a step anywhere yourself. The Fool just stands at the edge, admiring the sky, and never finds out where his own road would have led.

11-15-8.heading: Strong desires on fair terms
captions: Fair terms on time and money
paragraphs: Your desires are strong, and you care about handling them in the open. Justice shows in how you arrange your pleasures: you agree in advance, with yourself and with the people close to you, on time and spending, you do not hide what you buy, you split what is shared equally. The Devil feeds the pull itself — towards the delicious, the beautiful, the expensive, towards whatever grips the body and does not like to wait. Strength shapes the aftertaste: a calm dignity when desire has had its due without taking over.

**Your strength is that your pleasure stays honest — with others and with yourself.** The record collection grows within the agreed budget, dinner at a good restaurant is planned without secret excuses, and a shared holiday is chosen so that both of you will enjoy it. Then strong desire does not frighten you but brings joy: the lion walks beside you on a chain of flowers, and no one has to look away.

The scales, though, can be tipped in desire’s favour. You want more, and an argument turns up that sounds fair: I’ve worked hard, someone else treated themselves too, by rights it’s my due. Every pleasure becomes earned compensation, and any dispute about it becomes a hearing whose verdict is known in advance. The pull now rules through arguments. And after the purchase or the feast, instead of calm dignity you are left braced to defend yourself, as if someone were about to ask you to justify it.

16-9-7.heading: Leaving the common road to find your own pace
captions: A pull towards your own path
The thrill of your own momentum
paragraphs: A path of your own brings you more joy than the common one. The Tower clears it abruptly: the noisy club, hikes along the same old route, the usual weekend crowd — everything that rested on “that’s what everyone does” one day simply snaps. The Hermit explains where you are drawn: to a path where you can walk by your own light and work things out without prompting. The Chariot answers with excitement — you feel yourself moving, and that feeling is a joy in itself.

**Your free time feels full when you choose the route yourself and feel every step.** Say that instead of a group trip you set off by bike along country lanes where no one sets the pace. You have to find the way yourself, but every turn is yours. You come back with shining eyes and a story you want to share: others might find their way to where you have been.

A path of your own, though, easily becomes a source of pride. People who still go to the same club start to look stuck, and your stories about the country lanes quietly turn into a lesson: how it should be done, how people really live. You turn down invitations to group outings with a touch of condescension. Your friends stop asking, and excitement left without listeners demands fresh proof. The road keeps getting longer, while the joy you wanted to share grows ever scarcer along it.

16-18-7.heading: Turning into the unknown and steering in the dark
captions: The call of night and mystery
The thrill of crossing the unknown
paragraphs: Your usual way of spending free time can change in a single evening. The Tower knocks down what seemed reliable: familiar routes, a tried-and-tested crowd, holidays without surprises. Into the space it leaves, the Moon calls you — to places with little light and plenty of guesswork: a river at night, a cave, a forest after sunset, a strange city without a map. The Chariot turns this call into excitement: you steer through the unknown and feel yourself moving, even when you can see only a couple of steps of the road ahead.

**You delight in finding a way where none can be seen in advance.** Say that instead of a daytime tour you go on a night-time canoe trip: the water is black, the banks can only be guessed from their outlines, every bend in the river is a riddle. There is anxiety, but it sharpens you rather than freezing you. In the morning you are left with the feeling that you made it through the darkness under your own steam and have grown a little braver.

Yet any vague unease can start to look like a sign that it is time to change everything. Something feels murky inside — and you decide the pastime is to blame: you drop it, quickly find a new one, pick up speed again. The dash brings relief, but you never manage to work out what exactly was troubling you.
